text.tspan: Hands cultivate a garden with care.
A good way to care for a plant combines practical structure with an awareness of other people. Neither a rigid plan nor
complete improvisation is sufficient on its own; both need to be judged in context.
The practical case is straightforward: observing a plant helps us respond to what it needs. Consider how we check whether
the soil feels dry before adding water. The benefit is not merely efficiency. A modest arrangement prevents avoidable
confusion, leaving attention available for the activity itself rather than for problems that could have been anticipated.
Consideration adds a second, equally important dimension: keeping a simple record helps us learn from changes. In this
situation, we note which window gives the plant enough light without scorching its leaves. A decision can be convenient for
one person while creating difficulty for another, so its value depends partly on whose needs it recognises.
The most useful approach therefore brings structure and consideration together. Preparation establishes a workable starting
point; attention to other people keeps it responsive. Success should be assessed by how well the arrangement serves the
experience, rather than by how closely events follow the original plan.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a focused main idea. Develop one supporting reason in each body paragraph, with a concrete
example. Conclude by connecting the two reasons without introducing a new argument. Use the structure as a model; write
about an experience of your own.
Compare your first answer with this question: What two reasons support the main idea? Explain one example.
